title: The homogeneous core of a primary ideal is primary
statement: Let $R=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}R_d$ be a commutative ring graded by the nonnegative integers: every element has a unique finite sum of components in the additive subgroups $R_d$, $1\in R_0$, and $R_aR_b\subseteq R_{a+b}$. Assume $R$ is Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. Let $Q\subsetneq R$ be a primary ideal, meaning that $uv\in Q$ and $u\notin Q$ imply $v^h\in Q$ for some integer $h\ge1$. Define its homogeneous core by $Q^*=\{r\in R:\text{every homogeneous component of }r\text{ belongs to }Q\}$. Then $Q^*$ is a proper homogeneous primary ideal of $R$, contained in $Q$. Here homogeneous means closed under taking each homogeneous component, and primary has the same meaning as for $Q$.

source.place: Exercise 20.26, printed p.122, and its solution, printed p.229, using Proposition 20.24, printed p.122. Local PDF WANTED; authors PDF read online at https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed.pdf. Specialize the module statement to M=R.

proof.text: Put $H=Q^*$. Componentwise addition and negation show that $H$ is an additive subgroup. If $r=\sum_i r_i\in H$ and $s=\sum_j s_j\in R$, the degree-$d$ component of $sr$ is the finite sum $\sum_{i+j=d}s_jr_i$. Each summand lies in $Q$ since $r_i\in Q$, so $sr\in H$. Thus $H$ is an ideal. A component $r_i$ of an element of $H$ has its sole possibly nonzero component in $Q$, hence lies in $H$; this proves homogeneity. Also $r=\sum_i r_i\in Q$, so $H\subseteq Q$ and $H$ is proper. For a homogeneous $a$, the core formula gives $a\in H$ if and only if $a\in Q$.

source.place: Exercise 20.26, printed p.122, and its solution, printed p.229, using Proposition 20.24, printed p.122. Local PDF WANTED; authors PDF read online at https://web.mit.edu/18.705/www/13Ed.pdf. Specialize the module statement to M=R.

proof.text: Let $a,b$ be homogeneous, with $ab\in H$ and $a\notin H$. Step 1 gives $ab\in Q$ and $a\notin Q$. Since $Q$ is primary, $b^h\in Q$ for some $h\ge1$. If $b\in R_e$, repeated graded multiplication puts $b^h$ in $R_{he}$, so $b^h$ is homogeneous; the last assertion of step 1 therefore gives $b^h\in H$. This verifies the homogeneous-factor primary condition, including $b=0$ and degree zero.

Step 1 supplies that $H$ is a proper homogeneous ideal, and step 2 supplies exactly the criterion for homogeneous $a,b$. The cited statement yields primaryness for arbitrary factors $u,v\in R$. Together with the containment and homogeneity from step 1, this proves every clause.
